preamble: Prothesis or epenthesis of [h] involves the insertion of a glottal fricative before a vowel-initial word or syllable. This can occur as a grammatical marker (as in Celtic languages), as a way to avoid hiatus, or as a hypercorrection in dialects where [h] is regularly dropped (such as Cockney English). It is also seen in the historical development of Ancient Greek. A related environment is preaspiration, where [h] is inserted before a stop, as in Samic (Proto-Samic *kietë 'hand' > Northern Sami giehta).

examples.note: In some cases, initial vowels in Greek acquired a 'rough breathing' (h-), though this often reflects a lost *s- or *y-.
Grammatical h-prothesis: the 3rd person feminine possessive 'a' (her) triggers the insertion of [h] before a vowel-initial noun.
Hypercorrection: speakers of H-dropping dialects may insert [h] where it does not historically belong, especially when trying to speak formally.
Preaspiration: an [h] developed before strong-grade single stops and affricates in all Samic languages except Akkala, Kildin and Ter; South Sami gïete lacks it in this word.

examples.to: Northern Sami johka, Lule Sami jåhkå, South Sami johke
examples.note: Skolt Sami jokk shows a geminate instead.
